title: Taken up (Assumption, 15 August)
hook: defined in 1950, Catholics hold Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory (CCC 966)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven sorrows, from Simeon's prophecy to the tomb. Your line was a sword shall pierce thy soul.

In much of Europe, mid-August is when everything closes. In Italy it's called Ferragosto: shops shut, cities empty, families head to the beach. In France, Spain, Poland and plenty of other places, August fifteenth is a public holiday, and most tourists have no idea why. Ferragosto's name goes back to the Roman emperor Augustus, but the day itself is a feast of Mary, one of the oldest. Scripture doesn't tell us how Mary's life on earth ended. So where does the feast come from, and why did a pope in 1950 make it a formal teaching of the faith?
screen: `FERRAGOSTO: EVERYTHING CLOSES.` → `A FEAST OF MARY.` → `THE BIBLE IS SILENT.`

segments.voice: On November first, 1950, Pope Pius the Twelfth defined it: Mary, when the course of her earthly life was finished, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory. First he wrote to bishops all over the world asking what their people believed. The answer was overwhelming. Christians had been celebrating this in some form for well over a thousand years. Jesus ascended: he went up by his own power. Mary was assumed, from the Latin for taken up. She didn't rise by herself; she was received. And notice what the definition leaves out: whether Mary died first. Most Catholics, and the long tradition, say she did. Eastern Christians call the same August feast the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary. Catholics often point to a picture from the Book of Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." But the Church is honest that the teaching rests on tradition and the Church's faith, not one verse. The Catechism calls it a share in her son's resurrection and a preview of ours. In the Creed, Catholics say they believe in the resurrection of the body. Not escape from the body: the body, raised. The Assumption says that what God did for Jesus, he's already begun doing for one of us. In that view, your body, with its knees and scars and tiredness, isn't a shell. Catholics say it's part of you, and it's meant for glory.
screen: `NOVEMBER 1, 1950.` · `ASCENDED VS. ASSUMED.` · `THE DORMITION: FALLING ASLEEP.` · `A PREVIEW OF OUR RESURRECTION.` · then, large: `TAKEN UP BODY AND SOUL.`

segments.voice: Move your attention slowly up from your feet: legs, back, shoulders, hands, face, noticing where you're tired or sore or tight without judging any of it. Thank each part for carrying you today, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can thank God for your body, as it is; if you don't, just be kind to it for two minutes.
Assumption. From the Latin for taken up. Catholics hold Mary was taken body and soul into glory, a preview of the resurrection. Today's word.
Your line: the body matters. He ascended by his own power; she was taken up. That's day eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Assumption on 15 August, a holy day of obligation in many countries, and Eastern Christians keep the same day as the Dormition of the Mother of God.

chat.meaning: Pius the Twelfth defined it in 1950: Mary was taken up body and soul. She didn't rise by herself; she was received.

Ferragosto.meaning: Italy's mid-August holiday, named for Augustus

Assumption.meaning: from the Latin for taken up

Dormition.meaning: Eastern Christians' name: the falling asleep of Mary

Pius the Twelfth.meaning: the pope who defined it in 1950

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Revelation (Apocalypse) 12:1 given from memory; the DR book name is 'Apocalypse'. Confirm.
Munificentissimus Deus, 1 November 1950; Deiparae Virginis Mariae (1946) consulted the bishops. Confirm.
Feast 'well over a thousand years': the Dormition/Assumption feast was widespread by the 6th–7th centuries (Emperor Maurice fixed 15 August c. 600). Confirm.
'Most Catholics and the long tradition say she died': John Paul II (general audience, 25 June 1997) favored this view. Confirm phrasing.
Public holiday on 15 August in Italy, France, Spain, Poland and others. Confirm list.
'Taken up body and soul' in the teach screen paraphrases the definition; not presented as a quotation.

Audit (second sample): the hook implied Ferragosto exists because of the Assumption; the name and the mid-August holiday go back to Augustus's Feriae Augusti, later overlaid by the feast. Now says so. The teach's last lines stated a belief about the listener's body as fact; now attributed to Catholics.
